extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers learning probability, combinatorics, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook guidance on combinations, permutations, and the theory/rules of probability, combining conceptual foundations (probability as quantity of knowledge) with concrete calculation rules and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal rule for calculating probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Calculate the number of events which may happen independently of each other, and which, as far as is known, are equally probable. Make this number the denominator of a fraction, and take for the numerator the number of such events as imply or constitute the happening of the event, whose probability is required.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example: arrangements of the letters of 'Roma' are 4×3×2×1 = 24; seven of these are meaningful Latin words (Roma, ramo, oram, mora, maro, armo, amor), so the probability of a significant result is 7/24. Use this numerator/denominator counting method whenever equally likely cases can be enumerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combinations / arithmetical triangle for probability counts
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mathematical formulae of the theory are exactly the same as those of the theory of combinations... It is the comparative numbers of ways in which events can happen which measure their comparative probabilities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial counts (e.g., binomial coefficients from the arithmetical triangle) to compute probabilities: e.g., for three pennies, count eight total outcomes and use the triangle's entries to find probabilities for 0,1,2,3 tails (1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish comparative from absolute probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative probabilities compare relative numbers of ways events can occur (e.g., king vs diamond); absolute probabilities are measured as ratios of favorable to total equally-likely ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: four kings vs thirteen diamonds — probability of drawing a king is 4/52, a diamond 13/52, so their probabilities are proportional to their counts. Odds can be expressed from these ratios (e.g., odds against drawing a king are 48 to 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence rule — multiply probabilities of independent events
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the component events are independent, a simple rule can be given for calculating the probability of the compound event, — Multiply together the fractions expressing the probabilities of the independent component events.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: probability of two tails in two penny throws = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4; three tails in a row = 1/8. Multiplying numerators and denominators gives counts of favorable and total ways for the compound event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition rule for mutually exclusive events
rubrics_metrics.description: “Probabilities may be added to or subtracted from each other under the important condition that the events in question are exclusive of each other, so that not more than one of them can happen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add probabilities of events that are not mutually exclusive (doing so can produce absurd results). For exclusive events, sum their probabilities (or use odds-to-probability conversion when odds are given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of compound events and dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound event may be decomposed into two or more simpler events. Component events are independent when one happening does not alter the probability of another; otherwise they are dependent and must be treated accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of dependent sequence: firing a gun decomposed into pulling the trigger, fall of hammer, explosion of cap — these are not independent and their probabilities are not simply multiplied. Always check dependency before applying the independence multiplication rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as quantity of knowledge (conceptual foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability belongs to the mind and measures the 'quantity of knowledge' rather than an objective property of events ('chance'); 'an event is only probable when our knowledge of it is diluted with ignorance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use probability theory to guide and correct belief by quantifying knowledge vs ignorance. Do not conflate subjective belief states with the normative calculations of probability; the theory prescribes how belief ought to be distributed given information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental principle: distribute knowledge equally among similar cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Put similar cases on a par, and distribute equally among them whatever knowledge we have of one case may be affirmed of every case resembling it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this principle when symmetry or lack of distinguishing information makes cases equally probable (e.g., a fair coin: knowledge about head applies equally to tail). Adjust when evidence indicates asymmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update probabilities with experience and incorporate empirical information
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated trials supply information that changes our state of knowledge; e.g., many throws revealing a preponderance alter the probability estimate, and subsequent calculations must take such observed frequencies into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed frequencies (trials) to revise the set of equally-likely cases or to estimate biases (e.g., discover a loaded die). Probability theory guides inference when perfect measurement/trial to certainty is infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of certainty and impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is certain when all combinations give that event (probability = 1); an event is impossible when no combination gives it (probability = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat certainty as the ratio of a number to itself (1) and impossibility as 0 to some number (0). These are formal symbols expressing all-or-none combinatorial conditions, not mystical absolutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting permutations (n!) for arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of possible arrangements (permutations) of n distinct items is n×(n−1)×...×1 (n!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factorial counts when ordering matters: example, four letters produce 4×3×2×1 = 24 arrangements; combine this with selection of favorable arrangements to compute probabilities (as in the 'Roma' example).
